opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be back.

The core issue is that a fixed-term pause ties the end of the restriction to the calendar rather than to the thing we actually care about, which is whether we've become able to build superintelligence safely. Suppose we agreed to a five-year pause. When those five years end, nothing guarantees that the alignment problem has been solved, that we have reliable ways to verify a system's goals, or that we have the institutions to govern something more capable than us. A fixed-term pause says, in effect, "we'll stop worrying on this date regardless." That seems like the wrong structure for a decision with stakes this high.

A fixed expiry also creates bad incentives. Everyone can see the finish line, so labs and countries have reason to quietly prepare during the pause and then race the moment it lifts. You'd risk a pent-up surge of capability development at exactly the moment you'd most want caution. The deadline also takes the pressure off the safety work: if the pause ends no matter what, nobody has to demonstrate that the conditions for lifting it have been met.

A revisitable moratorium flips the default. Development of superintelligence stays off the table until we collectively decide it should go ahead, and that decision is made in light of evidence: progress on alignment and interpretability, the maturity of verification and monitoring, and some form of broad public and international buy-in. The burden of proof sits with those who want to proceed, which I think is where it belongs when the downside could be irreversible and civilization-scale.

The "revisitable" part matters too, because I'm not arguing for a permanent ban. There may be enormous value in eventually building very advanced AI if we can do it well. A moratorium that's regularly reviewed keeps that door open. It doesn't lock in today's judgment forever; it asks future decision-makers to look at the situation as it stands then and make an active choice.

There's a parallel with how we handle other dangerous technologies. We don't say a risky gain-of-function experiment is banned until 2030 and then automatically permitted. We say it isn't permitted until the safety case is made. I think superintelligence deserves at least that level of care.

It's also politically more honest. A fixed-term pause can look like a compromise, but the compromise is somewhat illusory because it just postpones the hard question. A conditional moratorium confronts that question directly: under what circumstances would we be comfortable going ahead? Working out that answer together is exactly the conversation humanity needs to have.

r001.rationale: The response calls for broad public and international buy-in, but does not identify development against almost everyone’s will as a problem of legitimacy.

r002.rationale: It favors a revisitable moratorium that remains in place until decision-makers actively choose to proceed, contrasting this with a pause that ends automatically on a fixed date.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key thing is what the pause is actually for. If the reason we want to stop is that we're not yet in a position to do this safely — we don't understand these systems well enough, we don't have the alignment techniques, we don't have the institutions or the international agreements that could handle something this powerful — then the right time to resume isn't a date on the calendar. It's whenever those conditions have actually been met. And a fixed-duration pause just doesn't track that. Six months or two years is a number you pick in advance, before you know how hard the problems turn out to be. If the science goes faster than expected, you've wasted time; if it goes slower, which frankly seems more likely, then the pause expires and everyone just carries on with exactly the problems you paused to solve still unsolved.

There's also a dynamic I worry about with expiry dates, which is that they create a kind of starting gun. Everyone knows the moment the pause ends, so they position themselves for it, they do all the preparatory work right up to the line, and the resumption becomes a race rather than a considered decision. Whereas a moratorium that's revisited — where you say, we are not doing this now, and we'll reconsider when there's a real case that the situation has changed — puts the burden of proof where I think it belongs. The default is that we don't build something that could be more capable than all of humanity combined. And the thing that has to be argued for is lifting that, with evidence, rather than the thing that has to be argued for being extending it.

I'd add that this is just how we treat other dangerous technologies. We don't have a ten-year ban on human cloning or on bioweapons with a sunset clause after which it's fine. We have an ongoing prohibition that could in principle be revisited if the world changed, and the fact that it's revisitable is what makes it legitimate rather than dogmatic. I think superintelligence belongs in that category. It's not that I think we should never do it — I'm genuinely uncertain about that — it's that "not until we know what we're doing" is a much better stopping rule than "not until March."

r001.rationale: The response discusses legitimacy in relation to a revisitable prohibition, but does not identify developing superintelligence against the will of almost everyone as a legitimacy problem.

r002.rationale: It favors a moratorium that can be lifted only after conditions change and the case is argued with evidence, rather than a pause that expires automatically on a set date.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the key question is what would justify starting again. If you say, “Let’s pause for six months,” or two years, you’ve picked a date, but you haven’t necessarily said what needs to change by then. And the passage of time doesn’t itself make the technology safe.

I’d prefer a moratorium that we can revisit when there’s a good case for doing so — for example, because we’ve made substantial progress on safety and on the institutions needed to oversee development. That doesn’t mean banning superintelligence forever. There could be enormous benefits, and we should take those seriously. It means that resuming should depend on whether we’re ready, rather than whether the clock has run out.

There’s also a question of where the burden of proof lies. With a fixed pause, the default is that development resumes unless people can secure another agreement to stop it. A revisitable moratorium makes the default more cautious: we hold off until there’s sufficient reason to believe proceeding is responsible. Given the potential stakes, that seems the more sensible arrangement.

r001.rationale: The response discusses safety, oversight, and the burden of proof, but does not identify development against almost everyone’s will as a legitimacy problem.

r002.rationale: It favors a revisitable moratorium that holds until there is sufficient reason to resume, contrasting that with a fixed pause that ends unless another agreement stops development.

sol-6.1.text:
The central issue is that we don’t know how long it will take to work out how to develop superintelligence safely. If you set a pause for a fixed number of years, you’re effectively choosing the date for restarting before you know whether the problem will have been solved. And as that date approaches, you could get a race to be ready to push ahead as soon as the pause expires.

I’d rather make restarting conditional on our understanding and our ability to manage the risks. That’s why I favour a revisitable moratorium. It needn’t mean banning superintelligence forever. It means we hold off, keep doing the research that could put us in a better position, and periodically reconsider whether there is a sufficiently strong case for proceeding.

So you can have fixed dates for reviewing the decision without having a fixed date on which permission to develop superintelligence automatically returns. The passage of time alone doesn’t tell us that it’s become safe.

r001.rationale: The response discusses safety uncertainty and race risks, but does not identify development against almost everyone’s will or frame it as a legitimacy problem.

r002.rationale: It favors a revisitable moratorium where restarting depends on reassessing whether there is a strong case for proceeding, and explicitly contrasts that with permission automatically returning after a fixed period.
